note: Craft and artistic traditions (making traditions: textiles, wood, metal, ceramics, glass, lacquer, paper, calligraphy, painting, carving, architecture, instrument making, clock and watchmaking, game-set making, puppetry and similar) moved out of the Possession taxonomy on 2026-10-31 (owner: they are artistic traditions, not products). Handed over as they stood, by source category. Objects stay in their categories as kinds; brands and makers stay in the brand registers. Food, origin and use traditions (food and drink, plants, healing, bathing, grooming and beauty, incense, falconry, breeding, fuel, fireworks) stay in the Possession taxonomy.

B2.auth: hand-spun undyed wool, natural dyes, irregular hand-drawn motifs and no drawn pattern

B2.d: Royal knotted-pile carpet weaving in the Turkish manner, developed into a French style under Crown monopoly.
B2.tech: Ghiordes knot, c. 90 knots per sq in
B2.auth: Crown property until 1768; dark grounds with medallions, bouquets and rinceaux

B2.d: Tapestry weaving in family workshops, also producing floral tapestry carpets; UNESCO intangible heritage since 2009.
Long-pile knotted wool covers, later floor rugs, wedding rugs and wall hangings (Finnish ryijy).
B2.tech: Ghiordes-type knot of three wool strands, long pile
B2.auth: mixed-shade three-strand knots; long pile; dated or initialled folk pieces

B2.d: Village and nomad flatweaving of kilims, named by town or tribe.
Double-sided wool kilims woven by hand on vertical looms.
B2.auth: Pirot geographical indication (2002); UNESCO ICH for Chiprovtsi (2014)

B2.d: Diné tapestry weaving of blankets and rugs, styled by trading post.
Felt carpets made by Kyrgyz women; on UNESCO's urgent-safeguarding list since 2012.
B2.tech: pressed felt (ala kiyiz), cut and stitched felt (shyrdak)

B2.d: Layered reused cloth stitched into quilts, throws and covers with running stitch and embroidered motifs.
B2.mat: old saris and dhotis; cotton, silk
B2.auth: Layered reused cloth, even running stitch and wavy gathered texture; 'kantha-stitched' commercial goods may be machine work.

B2.d: Improvised 'my way' piecing by African American women of an isolated river community.
B2.mat: old work clothes, fertiliser and flour sacks
B2.auth: Named maker and community provenance.

B2.r: Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, and other Amish settlements
B2.d: Bold, simply pieced quilts with intricate communal hand quilting.
B2.tech: machine or hand piecing, hand quilting
B2.auth: Community and date attribution; museum examples are often maker-unknown.

B2.n: North Country and Welsh wholecloth quilting
B2.r: County Durham, Northumberland, South Wales, Scottish Borders
B2.d: Quilts whose design is in the quilting, marked out by stampers or quilters; each region has its own motifs.
B2.auth: Regional motifs (Cable Twist, Weardale Chain, Plait); surviving blue pencil marking.

B2.d: Large single-motif appliqué quilts descended from kapa moe bark-cloth bedcovers.
B2.auth: One-piece fold-cut motif with outline quilting.

B2.d: Women's hand-made appliqué, patchwork and embroidered quilts.
B2.auth: Cotton hand work; synthetic cloth indicates later pieces.

B2.d: Running-stitch reinforcement and decoration of indigo cloth, also used on boro bedding.
B2.auth: Hand-stitched irregularity, aged indigo, layered repairs.

B2.d: Welsh woollen mills weaving reversible double-cloth tapestry blankets and bedspreads.
B2.auth: Pattern reversed in colour on each side; mill label; older pieces often two narrow widths seamed down the centre.

B2.d: English-woven wool trade blankets sold by the Hudson's Bay Company, sized by woven points.
B2.tech: heavy milled wool weaving with woven point marks
B2.auth: Points woven into the edge show size, not price; label with maker and points.

B2.d: Jacquard-woven wool robes and shawls made by mills for Native American customers, with patterns researched from tribal preferences.
B2.auth: Mill label; corner shape (round before 1909 at Pendleton, square after).

B2.d: Mexican weaving of long fringed sarapes brought north by Tlaxcalan weavers.
B2.mat: wool; machine yarn and synthetic dyes from the mid-1850s
B2.auth: Handspun yarn and natural dyes point to pieces before the mid-1850s.

B2.d: Backstrap-loom weaving of two-panel mantas with woven symbols, worn and used as carrying cloths.
B2.tech: backstrap loom, warp-faced pallay patterning, discontinuous warp
B2.auth: Two halves joined by a full-length decorated central seam.

B2.p: Meiji era (1868–1912) to present; brand renewed 2006
B2.d: Japan's largest towel-making district, whose certified towels must pass absorbency and quality tests.
B2.tech: terry weaving, yarn twisting, dyeing and finishing in some 200 local factories using soft river water
B2.auth: red-blue-white Imabari Towel certification label; 'made in Imabari' alone does not qualify

B2.d: Weaving of flat cotton hammam towels, with styles and colours varying by region.
B2.tech: flat weaving on manually operated looms
B2.auth: hand-loomed 100% cotton; traditional red with black or white lines

B2.p: Joseon dynasty (1392–1910); revived as art from the late 1960s
B2.d: Korean wrapping-cloth craft of patchwork, embroidered and single-piece cloths.
B2.tech: patchwork of sorted scraps with visible seams; embroidery; painting and gold foil
B2.auth: hand-stitched seams; natural fibres

B2.p: long tradition; flax imported since the 1950s–60s
B2.d: Linen yarn spun from 100% flax and fabric designed and woven in Ireland, now mostly luxury damask and plain linens.
B2.tech: linen weaving, damask and Jacquard weaving
B2.auth: Irish Linen Guild trademark; cloth woven abroad and only finished in Ireland may not carry it

B2.p: Middle Ages to present; geographical indication 2020
B2.d: Striped linen first woven as protective cloths for cattle, now table and kitchen linen.
B2.tech: striped weaving, traditionally by itinerant weavers
B2.auth: seven stripes; Basque linen geographical indication

B2.n: Rajasthani hand block printing (Bagru and Sanganer)
B2.r: Bagru and Sanganer, near Jaipur, Rajasthan, India
B2.d: Hand printing of cotton with carved wooden blocks and natural dyes by Chhipa printers.
B2.mat: cotton, natural dyes (indigo, madder, iron black)
B2.auth: GI tags: Sanganeri 2010, Bagru 2024; slight block-repeat irregularities

B2.d: Provençal printing of cotton with Indian-inspired motifs, banned in France 1686–1759.
Embroidered tribal textile made by brides as dowry; called suzandozi in Iran.

B2.r: Southeast Asia, South Asia, Central Asia, Japan, Americas
B2.d: Resist-dyeing of yarns before weaving so the pattern shows on both faces.
B2.auth: Both faces patterned, with slightly blurred design edges.

B2.d: Fabric printing of single-colour pastoral scenes on pale ground, named for Jouy-en-Josas.

B3.p: mid-18th century to present (records from the Keichō era)
B3.d: Hand-made lanterns of thin Mino washi over a fine bamboo frame, a designated Japanese traditional craft since 1995; the source of Noguchi's Akari.
B3.tech: bamboo strips wound on a mould, paper pasted (hari), designs stencilled or painted (surikomi), wooden parts finished (moriage); work split among specialists
B3.mat: Mino washi or silk, madake or hachiku bamboo, cedar, cypress or magnolia wood
B3.auth: double-layered upper ring hiding the shade joint; regional brandmark since 2006

B3.d: Lamp shades of cut coloured glass wrapped in copper foil and soldered over a mould, developed at Tiffany Studios.
B3.tech: watercolour design, paper patterns and numbered templates, glass cut and copper-foiled, soldered on a wooden mould
B3.mat: opalescent and coloured glass, copper foil, solder, bronze bases
B3.auth: copper-foil construction and Tiffany Studios attribution; most 'Tiffany lamps' are later Tiffany-style copies

B3.p: glassmaking confined to Murano from 1291; peak 15th–16th c.; revivals after 1866 and in the 1920s
B3.d: Venetian hot-worked soda glass, including chandeliers of hand-shaped flowers and leaves.
B3.tech: hot-working, filigrana, murrine, sommerso, gilding and enamel
B3.auth: 'Artistic Glass Murano' trademark (1994) certifies Murano manufacture; Asian and Eastern European imitations are common.

B3.p: from c. 1250; high Baroque fame 1685–1750; chandelier industry from 1724
B3.d: Clear potash and lead crystal, cut and engraved, including the Maria Theresa and crystal chandelier.
B3.tech: hand-cutting, wheel engraving, blowing, enamel painting
B3.auth: EU 'lead crystal' needs at least 24% lead oxide; lower-lead pieces are 'crystal glass'.

B3.p: Recorded from 1085; regional forms flourished in the Edo period
B3.d: Collapsible paper lanterns of washi stretched over a spiral split-bamboo frame that folds into its base.
B3.tech: Paper attached to the frame (hari), designs added (surikomi), powder on exposed wood (moriage); work often split between specialists
B3.mat: Washi (Mino, Nishinouchi), split bamboo, wood, copper or brass fittings
B3.auth: Gifu lanterns: designated traditional craft (1995) with a regional brandmark (2006); hand-applied washi on bamboo, not printed fabric or plastic

B3.p: Most prominent in the Ottoman era; made today
B3.d: Lamps whose blown-glass shades are covered in small hand-cut pieces of coloured glass.
B3.tech: Glass pieces glued by hand onto a clear blown globe, gaps filled with paste, shade fitted to a metal frame
B3.mat: Coloured glass, clear blown glass, beads, brass or bronze
B3.auth: Slight variation between pieces, deep colour when lit, heavy bronze base, glass rings when tapped (plastic copies sound dull)

B3.d: Brass lanterns cut or punched with geometric and floral openwork, often glazed with coloured glass.
B3.tech: Sheet brass pierced, hammered, chased and worked in repoussé; glass panes set in
B3.mat: Brass, coloured, seeded or etched glass
B3.auth: Many 'Moroccan-style' lanterns are made elsewhere (notably India); check origin and hand-cut rather than stamped work

B4.d: Venetian hot-worked glass, concentrated on Murano since 1291.
B4.tech: hot-working; millefiori, murrine, sommerso, filigrana, calcedonio
B4.auth: Artistic Glass Murano trademark (1994); Asian and Eastern European imitations are common

B4.d: Cut, engraved and coloured glass from the Czech lands.
B4.tech: wheel cutting and engraving, cased and coloured glass
B4.auth: maker marks; early Bohemian crystal contained no lead

B4.d: Moulded and frosted art glass in the manner of René Lalique.
B4.auth: 'R. LALIQUE FRANCE' mark and model number

B4.d: Art glass from the Småland glassworks, with Orrefors and Kosta as leading houses.
B4.tech: Graal, Ariel, Ravenna and Kraka techniques; engraving
B4.auth: engraved signature with technique and number

B4.d: Dutch tin-glazed earthenware painted in cobalt blue.
B4.tech: tin glaze over earthenware, painted in metal oxides
B4.auth: factory marks and monograms from c. 1640; 'Delfts Blauw' mark on Royal Delft

B4.d: Ottoman fritware painted under the glaze in cobalt, turquoise and bole red.
B4.tech: underglaze painting on fritware with white slip
B4.auth: style sequence: Abraham of Kütahya, Golden Horn, Damascus, Rhodian

B4.tech: hard-paste porcelain, overglaze enamels, underglaze blue
B4.auth: crossed swords mark (from 1720), variants help date pieces

B4.r: Lauscha, Thuringia, Germany (and Neustadt bei Coburg, Bavaria)
B4.d: Glassblowing town where moulded coloured glass ornaments and the glass bauble originated; exported worldwide from the 1840s.
B4.tech: Mouth- and mould-blown glass, silvered inside by hand and hand-painted; lamp-blowing into clay moulds, silver-nitrate silvering
B4.mat: Glass, silvering, paint, metal caps, silver nitrate
B4.auth: Mouth-blown with hand-silvered interior; Inge-Glas pieces carry the Star Crown (from 1987). Blown by one of the small family firms in Lauscha (about 20 in 2009).

B4.d: Wooden toy and Christmas-figure making that replaced declining ore mining around Seiffen.
B4.tech: lathe turning incl. Reifendrehen (ring turning), carving, painting
B4.auth: Maker's stamp or label from an Ore Mountains workshop; hand-turned and hand-painted parts

B4.d: Lathe-turned limbless dolls first sold by kijishi turners to hot-spring visitors, in regional styles tied to onsen.
B4.auth: Traditional pieces follow the shape and painting of their onsen style

B4.p: present centre Nusnäs; known abroad since 1939
B4.d: Carved pine horses painted in the kurbits style, a symbol of Dalarna and Sweden.
B4.tech: band-saw cutting, hand carving, kurbits painting
B4.auth: Hand-painted kurbits so no two are identical; maker's label from a Nusnäs workshop

B4.d: Nesting dolls turned in linden and painted in regional styles.
B4.auth: Turned, not carved from one block; regional painting style

B4.d: Festival dolls in Heian court dress displayed on tiers for Hinamatsuri.
B4.tech: carved and dressed doll making, from folded paper to carved figures
B4.auth: Arrangement follows Kantō or Kansai convention; court dress follows Heian style

B4.d: Papier-mâché daruma made from the charm moulds of Shōrinzan Daruma-ji.
B4.tech: papier-mâché over moulds, weighted base, painting

B4.d: Making decorated sweet-filled piñatas for Las Posadas and birthdays, a Mexican tradition traced to Acolman.
B4.tech: clay pot or cardboard/papier-mâché shell, often over a balloon, covered in crepe paper
ctr: San Juan de la Puerta, Guanajuato
B4.auth: hand-made shell and crepe-paper cones; traditional star form with seven points

B4.d: Industrial yet hand-painted terracotta gnome making that made Gräfenroda the centre of the garden gnome.
B4.tech: clay slip poured into moulds, kiln-fired and hand-painted
B4.auth: Fired, hand-painted terracotta from a Gräfenroda manufactory, not plaster, resin or plastic copies.

B4.d: Mouth-blown glass summer wind bells from Tokyo, painted from the inside.
B4.tech: glass blown without a mould; rim ground jagged for the ring; inside painting
B4.mat: glass, oil- and water-based paints, paper strip
B4.auth: uneven ground rim, painting on the inside, traditional vermilion-and-green strip

B4.d: Cast-iron ware of the old Nanbu domain, known for tea kettles and iron wind bells.
B4.tech: hand iron casting; some pieces finished with Joboji urushi
B4.auth: made in Morioka or Oshu by recognised workshops

B4.d: Paper cut with scissors or knives into symbols and animals, used on windows at festivals.
B4.auth: Hand-cut from a single sheet rather than printed; regional style differs

B5.r: Morioka and Mizusawa (Oshu), Iwate prefecture, Japan
B5.d: Sand-cast ironware tradition begun with tea-ceremony kettles for the Nambu domain, now covering tetsubin, pots, frying pans and omelette pans.
B5.tech: sand-mould casting, hand-finished; arare (hailstone) surface patterns; bare or blackened rust-resistant finish
B5.auth: Designated traditional craft; foundry marks of Iwachu/Oigen; fine-grain smooth casting; arare texture on kettles

B5.d: Norman 'city of copper' whose hammered copper and brass pans gave the town its name; home of Mauviel since 1830.
B5.tech: hammering and spinning of copper sheet, tin or stainless lining, riveted iron, bronze or stainless handles
B5.auth: Maker stamps (Mauviel 1830), gauge 1.5–2.5 mm, hammered or polished exterior, tin or stainless lining

B5.d: Porous, coarse-clay Iga stoneware whose heat-retaining body makes it the classic donabe material.
B5.tech: wood-fired climbing kilns; glazed interior, porous exterior
B5.auth: kiln mark; coarse unglazed exterior; sized in sun

B5.d: Yokkaichi semi-stoneware with high petalite content, giving flame-resistant donabe and teapots.
B5.tech: petalite-rich stoneware fired for thermal shock resistance
B5.auth: Yokkaichi-Banko marks; petalite body

B5.d: The 'Klingenstadt' tradition of forged swords, knives, scissors and razors behind Wüsthof, Zwilling, Böker, Güde and Herder.
B5.tech: drop-forging from a single blank with integral bolster, ice-hardening, hand finishing
B5.mat: X50CrMoV15 stainless, carbon steels, POM and wood handles
B5.auth: 'Solingen' is a protected origin mark; forged full tang, maker's trident/twins stamps

B5.d: French knife capital where about a hundred companies make seventy percent of French kitchen, table and pocket knives, including the Sabatier houses.
B5.tech: full forging, water-powered grinding historically, hand assembly
B5.mat: carbon and stainless steel, boxwood, olive, ebony, POM
B5.auth: 'Sabatier' alone is unprotected; look for registered house marks (K, Elephant, Lion, Diamant) and 'forgé à Thiers'

B5.d: Government-designated forged-blade craft: hand-forged, clay-quenched single-bevel knives made under a division of labour between smith, sharpener and handle fitter.
B5.tech: forge-welding steel to soft iron at ~900 °C, hand hammering, clay-coated water quench, hand sharpening and finishing
B5.mat: carbon steel (shirogami, aogami) on soft iron; magnolia handles with buffalo-horn ferrules
B5.auth: Sakai smith and sharpener marks; Tokugawa-era 'gokuin' quality stamp heritage; kasumi/hongasumi finish with urasuki hollow back

B5.d: Sword-making city since swordsmith Motoshige settled there; today Japan's volume centre for machine-forged stainless Western-style knives finished by hand.
B5.tech: machine stamping/forging and quenching, hand sharpening and handle fitting
B5.mat: stainless and powder steels (VG10, VG-MAX, molybdenum-vanadium), Swedish steels
B5.auth: 'Seki Japan' marks; Kai, Misono, Masahiro house stamps

B5.d: 700-year forged-blade tradition begun by Kyoto swordsmith Chiyozuru Kuniyasu making sickles; designated traditional craft, now centred on Takefu Knife Village.
B5.tech: hand forging of agricultural-tool heritage, prized toughness
B5.auth: Echizen Uchihamono Cooperative designation; maker mei from Takefu smiths

B5.d: Free-forged working blades from Shikoku's forestry and farming country: axes, sickles, hoes and rustic kurouchi kitchen knives in carbon steel.
B5.tech: free forging without moulds, hand hammering, kurouchi finish
B5.auth: rustic hand-forged kurouchi finish; Tosa cooperative labelling

B5.r: Tsubame and Sanjo, Niigata Prefecture, Japan
B5.d: Metalworking region begun with nails and farm hardware; Tsubame excels in precision stainless engineering, Sanjo in traditional hand forging.
B5.tech: Tsubame: stamping and precision stainless; Sanjo: hammer forging, nashiji and kurouchi finishes
B5.mat: stainless (CROMOVA, VG10), SKD/SLD semi-stainless, shirogami, aogami
B5.auth: maker mei; Sanjo forges' hand-ground finishes vs Tsubame machine precision

B5.d: Japan's oldest carpentry-tool region; chisel and plane-blade steel skills carried into small-volume kitchen knife making.
B5.tech: hand forging from carpentry-tool tradition, disciplined geometry and heat treatment
B5.auth: Miki maker marks

B5.d: Siliceous shale finishing stones quarried around Kyoto and used since the late 12th century for final sharpening of blades.
B5.tech: quarried and hand-cut natural stone, used with water and slurry for finish polishing
B5.mat: siliceous shale from the Tamba geological formation
B5.auth: natural stone with layered shale grain, free of mineral inclusions; graded by mine and hardness, no uniform synthetic texture

B5.r: Central Mexico (Puebla, Oaxaca and basalt regions)
B5.d: Hand-carving of tripod mortars and tejolote pestles from single blocks of vesicular basalt, continuing Aztec and Maya practice.
B5.tech: Chiselled from one block of porous basalt; interior left rough so worn bubbles keep renewing the grinding surface
B5.auth: Real basalt is porous, heavy and needs breaking in with rice; concrete imitations are smooth, lighter, shed grit and never season.

B5.d: Making of glazed stoneware mortars with combed kushi-no-me ridges inside, paired with wooden surikogi pestles, for sesame, miso and tororo.
B5.tech: Thrown bowl, exterior glazed, interior left unglazed and combed with radiating grooves before firing
B5.mat: Stoneware clay, glaze; sansho or other wood pestle
B5.auth: Unglazed combed interior in a ceramic body; plastic versions wear quickly and are not traditional.

B5.d: Unglazed purple, red and beige clay teapots made from clay near Lake Tai.
B5.tech: hand-built slab construction or slipcasting; high firing without glaze
B5.auth: maker's seals, clay colour and texture, hand-built vs slipcast; price depends on age, clay and artist

B5.d: Stoneware centre best known for red shudei kyusu.
B5.tech: stoneware, built-in clay sieves
B5.auth: potter's name and clay

B5.d: Hand-moulded, low-fired, porous tea bowls taken from the kiln while glowing hot.
B5.tech: hand shaping, low firing, lead glazes
B5.mat: clay, black, red and white glazes
B5.auth: attribution to Raku family generation

B5.d: Earthy tea ware with translucent beige glaze whose crazing darkens with use.
B5.tech: stoneware with kan-nyū crazing
B5.auth: glaze crazing darkened by use

B5.d: Korean-derived stoneware prized for tea-ceremony bowls.
B5.tech: iron underglaze painting, combined glazes
B5.auth: style (e-karatsu, Chōsen, madara)

B5.d: Stoneware with thick white glaze, red scorch marks and pinholes.
B5.tech: thick white shino glaze
B5.auth: glaze texture and scorch

B5.d: Hand-split bamboo tea whisks; designated a traditional craft in 1975.
B5.tech: eight-step hand splitting, shaving and thread binding
B5.auth: Takayama origin; about 120 types by school

B5.d: Main centre of Russian samovar making; 'Tula samovar' is the city's mark.
B5.tech: metalworking
B5.auth: 'Tula samovar' brand mark

B5.d: Japan's first porcelain, exported through Imari.
B5.tech: underglaze blue with overglaze enamels and gold

B5.d: Affordable everyday porcelain, once Japan's leading blue-and-white producer.
B5.tech: underglaze cobalt and celadon
B5.auth: sold under the Hasami ware label since 2002

B5.p: over 1,300 years; tea wares from 16th century
B5.d: Stoneware and porcelain making about half of Japanese pottery.
B5.tech: glazed stoneware (Shino, Oribe, Ki-Seto, Setoguro)

B5.d: Dutch tin-glazed earthenware painted mainly in cobalt blue.
B5.tech: tin glaze with underglaze cobalt
B5.auth: 'Delfts Blauw' hand-painted on the base

B5.d: French hard-paste porcelain from local kaolin, protected by a geographical indication.
B5.tech: hard-paste porcelain, overglaze decoration
B5.auth: Porcelaine de Limoges mark only for pieces made and decorated in Haute-Vienne (GI INPI-1702)

B5.d: Painted tin-glazed earthenware, first Italian centre to use lustre.
B5.tech: tin glaze, lustre

B5.d: Hand-thrown tin-glazed earthenware with six permitted natural colours.
B5.tech: wheel-thrown, twice fired, hand-painted
B5.auth: Denominación de Origen (1997): certified workshops' hologram and marks

B5.p: 1624 (Cutlers' Company) – present; Old Sheffield Plate 1740s–1840s; EPNS after 1840
B5.d: The English cutlery city: fused silver-on-copper 'Old Sheffield Plate', then electroplated nickel silver, alongside steel knives and canteens.
B5.tech: fused plate rolled from silver-clad copper ingots; later electroplating over nickel silver; forged and ground knife blades
B5.mat: sterling silver, copper, nickel silver, stainless steel
B5.auth: Old Sheffield Plate shows copper 'bleeding' at worn edges and has no hallmark; EPNS is stamped; 'Sheffield' marks are controlled by the Cutlers' Company.

B5.d: Electrolytic silver plating brought to France when Charles Christofle bought the Ruolz and Elkington patents in 1842.
B5.tech: electroplating of silver onto nickel-silver or copper blanks
B5.auth: Christofle pieces carry the house hallmark and plating-grade numerals; the company publishes a hallmark guide.

B5.d: Nuribashi from Obama on Wakasa Bay: wood built up in natural lacquer with shell, pine needle and eggshell inlay, then polished to reveal the pattern.
B5.tech: multiple lacquer layers over inlay, ground back and polished
ctr: Obama workshops (about ten master craftsmen remain)
B5.auth: Genuine Wakasa pairs show inlay revealed through ground lacquer rather than printed patterns.

B5.d: Tokyo hand-planed hardwood chopsticks in square to octagonal sections, sized to the user's grip.
B5.tech: hand planing of hardwood; rounded tips
B5.mat: ebony, red sandalwood, ironwood, Japanese box, maple
B5.auth: Unlacquered precious hardwood with visible hand-planed facets; the name was coined by Daikokuya in 1999.

B5.p: Technique established early Edo period; oldest surviving piece 1524
B5.d: Japanese lacquerware on wooden cores with an unusually durable layered undercoat.
B5.tech: many layers of urushi mixed with powdered diatomaceous earth (ji-no-ko) over wood
B5.auth: ji-no-ko undercoat on solid wood; Wajima-style pieces are also made by overseas workshops

B5.d: Cut-glass craft of Tokyo with overlay colour glass cut in fine geometric patterns.
B5.tech: Coloured overlay blown over clear glass, marked, rough- and fine-cut on wheels, polished
B5.mat: Clear or lightly tinted glass with coloured overlay
B5.auth: Designated Tokyo Traditional Craft (1985) and National Traditional Craft (2002); traditional patterns such as nanako

B5.d: Cut, engraved and painted glass and crystal of Bohemia, prized since the Renaissance.
B5.tech: Wheel cutting and engraving, blowing, painting, reverse glass painting
B5.mat: Potash-chalk glass; lead crystal in later work
B5.auth: Maker's marks of named glassworks; potash-chalk composition in early pieces

B5.r: Laguiole and Thiers, Massif Central, France
B5.d: Occitan slipjoint pocket-knife tradition, first designed by Jean-Pierre Calmels in 1829, which added the corkscrew in 1880 for Auvergnat café owners and gave rise to the sommelier knife.
B5.tech: forged blade and backspring, hand-fitted slipjoint, decorated spring and forged bee
ctr: Laguiole village (Forge de Laguiole, Honoré Durand)
B5.auth: Name is not legally protected; look for named workshop, hand-finished spring and bee, made-in-France marking.

B5.d: Korean earthenware jars, unglazed or dark-brown glazed, used for fermenting and storing kimchi, soy sauce and pastes.
B5.tech: Coil-built earthenware fired at 600–700 °C unglazed or over 1100 °C with dark-brown glaze; slightly porous body lets ferments breathe.
B5.auth: Hand-thrown body, dark brown glaze, breathable walls; look for size names and workshop marks rather than mass-moulded uniformity.

B5.d: Steam-bent Akita-cedar woodware, best known for lightweight bento boxes with straight grain and warm colour.
B5.tech: Steam bending of thin cedar boards, joined with cherry-bark stitching
ctr: Ōdate woodcutters; craft encouraged by Satake Nishiie, Lord of Ōdate Castle
B5.auth: Ōdate origin, straight-grained Akita cedar, bark-stitched seam, unfinished or urushi-coated interior

C1.p: Edo period onward (wide ripsaws from 1763); higonokami 1896–present
C1.d: Miki smithing tradition of carpentry blades—saws, chisels, planes, knives and large construction tools.
C1.tech: forge-welding carbon steel to iron with borax flux, forging, annealing in straw ash, water quench, two-stage tempering, polishing
C1.auth: laminated hard-steel edge on softer iron; smith's stamp

C1.d: Natural Japanese waterstones (tennen toishi) quarried for finishing blades, used wet.
C1.tech: quarried and cut stone used with water

C1.d: France's main cutlery centre, making about 70% of the country's cutting tools, including laguiole and Douk-Douk knives.
C1.tech: forged or stamped blades, slip-joint assembly
C1.mat: carbon and stainless steel, horn, wood
C1.auth: 'Laguiole' is not a protected name; French makers stamp their mark, steel or 'Made in France' on the blade.

H4.d: Interwar export trade in figural and cut perfume bottles drawing on centuries of Bohemian glassmaking.
H4.tech: press-moulded stoppers, mould-blown bases, selective polishing, intaglio, enamelling, jewelled metal mounts
H4.auth: 'Made in Czechoslovakia' acid stamp on the base; Turriet & Bardach metal stamped Austria; post-war Glassexport bottles usually lack the stamp; Hoffmann reproductions often have a different base shape.

H4.d: Mouth-blown decorative bottles sold for perfume oils, notably in the perfume shops of Khan el-Khalili.
H4.tech: free blowing with a blowpipe; neck and stopper formed by hand
H4.auth: Hand-made pieces vary in height and shape from bottle to bottle.

J10.d: Town of the French Jura that became a centre of briar pipe manufacture from about 1854.
Free-form carving of briar to the grain, from Sixten Ivarsson's Copenhagen workshop and its pupils.
J10.auth: Maker's signature or stamp on the shank.

J10.d: Carving of sepiolite pipes from the Eskişehir deposits.
J10.tech: Hand carving of soft sepiolite, then hardening by drying
J10.auth: Carved block rather than pressed pieces.

J10.d: Metal smoking pipe for kizami tobacco, an Edo-period status object now made by few artisans.

J10.d: Status objects of the Qing court and elite, made in glass, porcelain, hardstone and enamel.
J10.tech: Glass blowing and overlay, porcelain, hardstone carving, inside painting
J10.mat: Glass, porcelain, jade, agate, amber, coral, ivory
J10.auth: Original stopper and spoon rarely survive; imperial pieces are most prized.
